passage.title: Carved by a Single Drop
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Deep beneath grassy hills and forest floors, giant rooms of stone sit in total darkness. These underground halls are called limestone caves. No human builders ever swung a pickaxe or shovel to dig them out. Instead, plain rainwater did all the work over thousands of years. As rain falls through the sky and soaks into dead leaves on the ground, it picks up carbon dioxide gas. This gas turns the water into a weak acid that does not burn skin, though it can dissolve soft rock.

Drops of this weak acid seep down through thin cracks in the gray limestone. Year after year, the moving water eats away tiny bits of stone along each split. Thin cracks slowly grow into tunnels, and small tunnels join to form huge chambers. At first, groundwater fills the entire space from floor to ceiling. Later, when nearby rivers cut deeper into the valley, the water drains out and leaves an empty cave filled with air.

Once air fills the cave, the same dripping water begins to build new rock shapes instead of carving them away. Each drop that seeps through the cave roof carries dissolved mineral from the limestone above. When a drop hangs from the ceiling and meets the cave air, it loses a bit of gas. A tiny ring of solid mineral, left behind on the stone ceiling before the water falls, is slowly built up by thousands of drops into a hanging stalactite. It looks like a stone icicle pointing straight down.

The work of that single drop does not end when it lets go of the ceiling. The falling drop splashes onto the cave floor directly below the tip of the stalactite. There, it leaves one more tiny speck of mineral on the ground. Over centuries, these floor specks stack up to form a thick cone called a stalagmite. Cave guides tell the two apart by remembering that stalactites hold tight to the ceiling, while stalagmites might reach the roof.

At times, a hanging cone and a rising cone grow long enough to meet in the middle. When they fuse together, they form a solid stone pillar from floor to ceiling. Cave rocks grow so slowly that a single inch of new stone can take more than a hundred years to form. Because skin oils from human fingers stop mineral rings from sticking to the wet stone, park rangers ask visitors to never touch a cave wall.

tier2Words.definition: to melt or break down a solid substance into tiny invisible parts inside a liquid
tier2Words.contextClue: The weak acid does not burn skin, but it can break down soft limestone rock as it seeps through cracks.

tier2Words.definition: to flow or leak slowly through small openings or porous material
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old English sipian, meaning 'to soak or trickle slowly'
tier2Words.contextClue: Trickles of water leak slowly downward through narrow cracks in the gray limestone bedrock.

tier2Words.definition: large enclosed rooms or open spaces, especially underground
tier2Words.contextClue: Narrow cracks widen into tunnels, and small tunnels join to form huge underground rooms.

tier2Words.definition: to join or blend two separate things together into a single solid piece
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin fundere, meaning 'to melt or pour together'
tier2Words.contextClue: When a hanging stalactite and a rising stalagmite meet in the middle and join together, they form a solid stone column.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"A tiny ring of solid mineral, left behind on the stone ceiling before the water falls, is slowly built up by thousands of drops into a hanging stalactite."

Based on the structure of the sentence, what builds the tiny ring of solid mineral into a hanging stalactite?

options.text: Park rangers build the mineral rings using special cave tools.
options.childFeedback: Park rangers are only mentioned in Paragraph 5 asking visitors not to touch cave walls; human builders never make the mineral rings.

options.text: The stone ceiling builds thousands of water drops before they fall.
options.childFeedback: This flips the action around! The stone ceiling simply holds the mineral ring while thousands of water drops slowly build it up.

options.text: A hanging stalactite builds the stone ceiling out of rainwater.
options.childFeedback: A stalactite is the icicle-shaped rock that gets built over time—it does not build the stone ceiling out of rainwater.

options.text: Thousands of drops build the tiny ring of mineral into a stalactite.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by thousands of drops' right after 'is slowly built up' shows that thousands of dripping water drops build the mineral ring into a hanging stalactite.

questions.provingSentenceText: A tiny ring of solid mineral, left behind on the stone ceiling before the water falls, is slowly built up by thousands of drops into a hanging stalactite.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by thousands of drops' right after 'is slowly built up' shows that thousands of dripping water drops build the mineral ring into a hanging stalactite.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'A tiny ring of solid mineral' receives the action, while the prepositional phrase 'by thousands of drops' identifies the agent that builds the stalactite.
questions.retryHint: Look for the 'by' phrase after 'is slowly built up' in Paragraph 3 to see what builds the mineral ring.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 5:

"At times, a hanging cone and a rising cone grow long enough to meet in the middle. When they fuse together, they form a solid stone pillar from floor to ceiling."

What does the word fuse mean as it is used in Paragraph 5?

options.text: Crack apart into tiny grains of gray sand
options.childFeedback: Cracking apart into sand is the opposite of what happens in Paragraph 5, where the two cones join together into one solid stone column.

options.text: Drip quickly from a high stone roof
options.childFeedback: Water drops drip from the roof earlier in the passage, but in Paragraph 5 'fuse together' describes what the two rock cones do when they meet.

options.text: Join and bond into one solid piece
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 5, 'fuse' means to join and bond into one solid piece, because the hanging cone and rising cone meet in the middle to form one solid stone column from floor to ceiling.

options.text: Shine brightly in a dark underground room
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 says underground limestone caves sit in total darkness, so the stone cones do not shine brightly when they meet.

questions.provingSentenceText: When they fuse together, they form a solid stone pillar from floor to ceiling.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 5, 'fuse' means to join and bond into one solid piece, because the hanging cone and rising cone meet in the middle to form one solid stone column from floor to ceiling.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 5 explains that a stalactite and stalagmite grow until they meet in the middle and form a single solid stone pillar, showing that 'fuse' means to join or bond into one piece.
questions.retryHint: Look at what happens in Paragraph 5 when the hanging cone and rising cone meet in the middle to form a single solid stone column.

questions.prompt: According to Paragraph 1, how does plain rainwater gain the ability to dissolve solid limestone rock?

options.text: It heats up to a boiling temperature as it flows past deep underground rivers.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 never mentions boiling temperatures or hot underground rivers; a gas from the air and dead leaves is what turns the rainwater acidic.

options.text: It picks up carbon dioxide gas from the air and dead leaves, turning into a weak acid.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 explains that as rainwater falls through the air and soaks through dead leaves on the ground, it picks up carbon dioxide gas, which turns it into a weak acid that dissolves limestone.

options.text: It mixes with skin oils left behind by visitors walking on the forest floor.
options.childFeedback: Human skin oils are mentioned in Paragraph 5 because they stop mineral rings from sticking to cave walls, not because they help rainwater dissolve rock.

options.text: It carries sharp pebbles that scrape the cave walls during heavy summer floods.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 states that carbon dioxide gas turns rainwater into a weak acid that dissolves soft rock, not that sharp pebbles scrape the walls.

questions.provingSentenceText: As rain falls through the sky and soaks into dead leaves on the ground, it picks up carbon dioxide gas.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 1 explains that as rainwater falls through the air and soaks through dead leaves on the ground, it picks up carbon dioxide gas, which turns it into a weak acid that dissolves limestone.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 states that rainwater picks up carbon dioxide gas from the sky and dead leaves on the ground, which turns the water into a weak acid capable of dissolving limestone.
questions.retryHint: Check the last two sentences of Paragraph 1 to see what rainwater picks up from the sky and dead leaves.

questions.prompt: In Paragraph 5, why does the author explain the effect of human skin oils on wet stone?

options.text: To support the point that cave visitors should never touch cave formations
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 5, the author explains that oils from human fingers stop new mineral rings from sticking to wet stone in order to show why park rangers ask visitors never to touch cave walls.

options.text: To prove that human skin is stronger than weakly acidic rainwater
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 mentions that the weak acid does not burn skin, while Paragraph 5 focuses on how finger oils harm growing cave rocks.

options.text: To show how park rangers polish stalactites so they look like stone icicles
options.childFeedback: Park rangers do not polish stalactites; they ask people not to touch the wet stone so minerals can keep sticking and growing naturally.

options.text: To argue that all underground caves should be closed to every scientist
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 only says visitors are asked not to touch the cave walls, not that every underground cave should be closed to scientists.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because skin oils from human fingers stop mineral rings from sticking to the wet stone, park rangers ask visitors to never touch a cave wall.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 5, the author explains that oils from human fingers stop new mineral rings from sticking to wet stone in order to show why park rangers ask visitors never to touch cave walls.
questions.parentExplanation: In alignment with ELAGSE5RI8 (author's reasons and evidence), the author gives the scientific reason—skin oils prevent mineral rings from sticking—to support the rule that visitors must not touch cave walls.
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 5 to see how the fact about skin oils connects to the park rangers' rule for visitors.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which claim does the author make in Paragraph 3 about how water's role in a cave changes over time?

options.text: Once air enters a cave, rainwater loses all of its minerals and can no longer drip from the roof.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 says each drop loses a tiny bit of gas when it meets the air, which causes it to leave solid mineral behind—not lose its ability to drip.

options.text: Once air fills an empty cave, dripping water switches from carving away rock to building new rock shapes.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 states that once the cave drains and fills with air, dripping water changes jobs—instead of carving rock away, it leaves tiny mineral rings behind to build new rock shapes.

options.text: Water can only form stalactites when the entire cave chamber is completely flooded from floor to ceiling.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain the opposite: water carves out the cave while it is flooded, and stalactites only start forming after the water drains and air fills the space.

options.text: Dripping water builds a full-sized stone pillar from floor to ceiling in less than one week.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 says cave rocks grow so slowly that just one inch of new stone can take more than a hundred years, never less than a week.

questions.provingSentenceText: Once air fills the cave, the same dripping water begins to build new rock shapes instead of carving them away.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 states that once the cave drains and fills with air, dripping water changes jobs—instead of carving rock away, it leaves tiny mineral rings behind to build new rock shapes.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 opens with the key claim that once water drains and air fills the cave, the dripping water shifts from dissolving/carving limestone to depositing calcite minerals that build new formations.
questions.retryHint: Read the first sentence of Paragraph 3 to see what dripping water begins to do once air fills the cave.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "No human builders ever swung a pickaxe or shovel to dig them out."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 1 only explains that humans did not dig the cave, without showing how water switches from carving rock to building it.

options.text: "At first, groundwater fills the entire space from floor to ceiling."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 2 only describes the early flooded stage of the cave before the water drains out and air enters.

options.text: "The falling drop splashes onto the cave floor directly below the tip of the stalactite."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 4 describes where a falling drop lands on the floor, rather than explaining the big switch in water's role once air fills the cave.

options.text: "Once air fills the cave, the same dripping water begins to build new rock shapes instead of carving them away."
options.childFeedback: This opening sentence from Paragraph 3 directly proves Question 5 by stating that once air fills the cave, dripping water starts building new rock shapes instead of carving them away.

questions.provingSentenceText: Once air fills the cave, the same dripping water begins to build new rock shapes instead of carving them away.
questions.childTip: This opening sentence from Paragraph 3 directly proves Question 5 by stating that once air fills the cave, dripping water starts building new rock shapes instead of carving them away.
questions.parentExplanation: Option C is the exact sentence in Paragraph 3 that states how water transitions from carving rock to building new rock shapes once air fills the cave.
